title: Building academic vocabulary
lines: Vocabulary affects every section. In Reading you need it for Complete the Words and vocabulary-in-context questions; in Listening it helps you follow academic talks; in Writing and Speaking it lets you express ideas precisely. The good news is that a few hundred high-frequency academic words appear again and again across subjects. Learn those well and the test becomes much easier.
## Which words to learn

- General academic words: words used in every subject, such as analyze, significant, assume, factor, approach, evidence, decline, contribute, consequence, distinct, interpret, sufficient. These are your top priority.

- Topic words: the basic terms of common TOEFL subjects (biology, geology, astronomy, history, psychology, economics, art). You do not need specialist knowledge, but words like species, sediment, orbit, settlement, behavior and demand should not surprise you.
- Campus words: words for university life, such as enrollment, deadline, advisor, prerequisite, transcript, dormitory, extension and tuition. These appear in conversations, announcements and emails.
- Signal words: however, therefore, whereas, nevertheless, in contrast, as a result. They show how ideas connect and help you answer purpose and inference questions.
## Learn word families, not single words
Complete the Words tests whether you can finish a word correctly in context, and that depends on the right form. Learn each word with its family.
> analyze (verb), analysis (noun), analyst (person), analytical (adjective)
> vary (verb), variation (noun), variety (noun), various (adjective), variable (adjective, noun)
> economy (noun), economic (adjective, about the economy), economical (adjective, saving money), economist (person)
! Watch for pairs that look alike but mean different things: economic/economical, historic/historical, sensible/sensitive, affect (verb)/effect (noun).
## Learn words in sentences
A word list with translations is a start, but you remember a word much better when you meet it in a sentence. For each new word, write one sentence of your own about your own life or studies.
> "The survey found a significant increase in the number of students cycling to campus."
## Synonyms for vocabulary-in-context questions

Reading questions ask which word is closest in meaning to a word in the passage. The correct option fits the sentence's meaning, not just the dictionary entry. Learn one to three synonyms for each key word, and always check the sentence.
> "The new policy had a marked effect on attendance." Here marked means noticeable or clear, not "written on".
## Collocations for writing and speaking
Collocations are words that naturally go together. Using them makes your writing and speech sound natural.
- make a decision, make progress, make an effort (not do a decision)
- do research, do homework, do damage
- conduct an experiment, raise a question, draw a conclusion
- play a role in, have an impact on, pay attention to
- strongly agree, highly effective, widely used
## A daily vocabulary routine (15-20 minutes)
- Learn 10 new words with the flashcards in this app: meaning, word family, one synonym.
- Review yesterday's words and the words from three days ago and one week ago. Spaced review is the most efficient way to remember.
- Write two sentences using today's words.
- When you read or listen to anything in English, note one or two academic words you meet and add them to your list.
! Ten words a day with honest review beats fifty words a day that you forget by the weekend.
## Guessing meaning from context
You will always meet some unknown words. Use the context:
- Look for a definition or example nearby ("such as", "that is", "in other words").
- Look for contrast ("unlike", "but") which tells you the word means the opposite of something you know.
- Look at word parts: un-, in-, dis- (not), re- (again), pre- (before), -able (can be), -less (without).
> "Unlike the gregarious meerkat, the leopard is largely solitary." If solitary means alone, gregarious must mean social, living in groups.
## Using vocabulary in Writing and Speaking

Do not try to fill your email or discussion post with rare words. Use words you are sure of, correctly. One precise word ("this would reduce traffic") is better than an impressive wrong one. Aim for variety: if you have written "important" twice, try "essential", "crucial" or "significant" the third time.
